strengths: Introduces a novel, well-curated benchmark (GIQ) spanning a wide taxonomy of polyhedra (Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, Kepler-Poinsot, stellations, compounds) with mathematically precise ground-truth properties, addressing a real gap in existing 3D benchmarks like Objaverse that lack fine-grained symmetry/geometry annotations.

Substantial data collection effort: 224 unique shapes rendered synthetically plus physically constructed paper models photographed under varied indoor/outdoor real-world conditions, providing a useful sim-to-real testbed.

Comprehensive multi-task evaluation covering four complementary facets of geometric reasoning (monocular reconstruction, symmetry probing, mental rotation, zero-shot VLM classification), touching diverse model families (reconstruction models, self-/supervised encoders, multi-view geometry networks, frontier VLMs, geometry-native 3D LLMs).

Inclusion of a human baseline user study for the mental rotation task strengthens the claims by contextualizing model performance against human performance rather than relying on accuracy numbers alone.

Findings are interesting and diagnostic: strong linear probe performance for symmetry detection contrasts with poor performance on fine-grained mental rotation and VLM shape classification, illustrating a nuanced picture of implicit vs. explicit geometric understanding.
Qualitative error analysis of VLM failures (confusing convexity, conflating compounds/stellations, hallucinating faces) adds interpretability beyond aggregate accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: Much of the quantitative evidence is deferred to the appendix (e.g., reconstruction is only shown qualitatively for 3 shapes in the main text with no numerical metrics like Chamfer distance or IoU), weakening the self-contained rigor of the main paper.
The reconstruction evaluation is limited to only three representative shapes, which is a small and possibly non-representative sample for concluding broad failure across complexity levels.

The paper is primarily an evaluation/benchmark study using existing off-the-shelf methods (linear/non-linear probes, pretrained reconstruction and VLM models) without proposing new techniques or remedies, limiting technical novelty despite the useful diagnostic contribution.
Some categorization choices are acknowledged as arbitrary by the authors themselves (overlapping counts, e.g., 238 vs 224), which could affect reproducibility/clarity of exact task splits.

Sample sizes per polyhedron category for zero-shot VLM classification are not clearly reported in the main text, making it hard to assess the statistical reliability of category-wise accuracy differences.

No experiments explore whether fine-tuning or targeted training (rather than just probing/zero-shot evaluation) could close the observed geometric reasoning gaps, limiting the paper's actionable insights beyond diagnosis.
The redacted phrase regarding who constructed the physical models suggests some incomplete anonymization/preparation of the manuscript.

Only a single fixed prompt is used for the primary VLM classification, and while CoT/multi-view ablations are attempted, the exploration of prompting strategies remains fairly limited given known prompt-sensitivity of VLMs.
